1044.title: Rebecca Gratz
1044.hook: founded the first Jewish Sunday school in America in 1838
1044.howItsDone: Synagogues in America run weekend or after-school religious schools where volunteer and part-time teachers teach Hebrew, prayer, Bible, holidays and history, a model often traced to Rebecca Gratz's Hebrew Sunday School in Philadelphia.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Grace Aguilar, and your line: a woman's voice. Today, one last woman for this stretch, a teacher across the ocean in Philadelphia.

Sunday morning in Philadelphia. Church bells. Children in their best clothes walking to Sunday school, lesson books under their arms. And a few Jewish children watching them go, or walking along with their friends, because there is no Jewish school for them to go to. A woman named Rebecca Gratz notices, and asks a practical question: why not a school for Jewish children, on the day they're free? In 1838, her answer gets its first class.
screen: `SUNDAY MORNING, PHILADELPHIA.` → `NO SCHOOL FOR JEWISH CHILDREN.` → `WHY NOT ONE OF OUR OWN?`

segments.voice: Rebecca Gratz was already busy. From a well-known Jewish family in Philadelphia, she had spent years building things for people in need: a society to help orphans, a society of Jewish women to help poor Jewish families. She never married, and she helped raise her sister's children after their mother died. Then came the school she called the Hebrew Sunday School. A school on Sunday was an idea her Christian neighbors already used, and she saw no reason Jewish children couldn't have it too, filled with their own Bible, their own prayers, their own history. The teachers were young Jewish women, volunteers. They had few books, so they made do, and some wrote the lessons themselves. The children came. Behind it is a command the Torah gives every parent, in the Shema itself: "and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way." Rebecca Gratz asked: and when the parents can't, who will? The school answered: the community will, and women would teach. Her model, a weekend Jewish school run by the community, spread to other cities, and versions of it still exist in synagogues today. People also tell a story that she was the model for the Jewish heroine Rebecca in Walter Scott's novel Ivanhoe. Nobody has proven it. What can be shown is quieter: a woman, a free morning, and children who learned their own story.

segments.voice: Hold a child in your life in mind, your own, a relative, a neighbor, a student, and one small thing you know that they don't yet: how to tie a knot, a family story, a blessing, why the moon changes shape. Picture telling them, where you'd sit and what they'd ask. If you pray, you can hold that child in your prayer; if not, simply hold them in mind.

1045.title: About fifteen million
1045.hook: Jews today live mostly in Israel and North America, with communities worldwide
1045.howItsDone: Some communities gathering a minyan avoid counting people by number, saying "not one, not two" or counting with the words of a verse; population estimates are made by demographers, who note that the answer depends on who is counted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rebecca Gratz, and your line: sunday school. That closes the women's stretch. Now, Jewish life today, starting with a count.

Some prayers need a minyan, a quorum, so someone at the door has to count heads. And in some synagogues, the person counting won't say one, two, three. Some say, not one, not two, not three. Some count by the words of a verse, one word per person. It sounds like a quirk. It's actually a very old instinct: be careful about counting people like objects. Keep that in mind, because today's title is a number, and an enormous one: about fifteen million.
screen: `COUNTING FOR A MINYAN.` → `NOT ONE, NOT TWO.` → `A VERY OLD CAUTION.`

segments.voice: The caution goes back to the Torah. When Moses is told to take a census, each person gives half a shekel of silver, so that no plague comes among them. The rabbis read it this way: count the coins, not the heads. Later, when King David counts the people directly, the book of Samuel tells of a plague that follows. Behind both stories sits a conviction: a person is not a unit. And there's an older promise. God takes Abraham outside at night and says: "Look now toward heaven, and count the stars, if thou be able to count them." The point of that count is that you can't finish it. Now the modern number: about fifteen million Jews in the world. It's an estimate, not a head count, because counting Jews raises real questions. Who counts? Movements answer differently. Orthodox and Conservative Judaism count a person Jewish through a Jewish mother or a conversion under Jewish law; Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism in North America also count a child of one Jewish parent who is raised Jewish. Some people with Jewish roots don't call themselves Jewish; some who do, others wouldn't count. So the number comes with an asterisk. Where do they live? Mostly in Israel and North America, then in communities around the world: France and Britain, Argentina and Brazil, Russia and Ukraine, South Africa, Australia, Morocco, India and elsewhere, some large, some a handful of families with one old synagogue. Big enough to fill cities, small next to the stars. Each one a name, not a unit.

1046.title: Jews by choice
1046.hook: converts, like Ruth, are fully Jewish; reminding them of their past is forbidden
1046.howItsDone: Conversion to Judaism involves study with a rabbi and usually appearing before a rabbinic court, and often immersion in a mikveh; movements differ in their requirements, and Jewish law forbids reminding a convert of their past.

segments.voice: Yesterday, minyan, and your line: fifteen million, a big number counted with care. Today, some of those faces arrived by choosing.

A dusty road out of Moab. Three widows walking. The oldest, Naomi, is going home to Bethlehem, and she tells her two daughters-in-law to go back to their own mothers. Orpah kisses her and goes, and the text doesn't blame her. Ruth holds on, and tells her: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Today is about people who say that sentence with their lives.
screen: `THREE WIDOWS ON A ROAD.` → `ORPAH GOES HOME.` → `RUTH HOLDS ON.`

segments.voice: Jewish tradition reads Ruth as a convert, someone not born Jewish who chose to join the people and its God. Hebrew calls such a person a ger tzedek, a righteous convert. The word ger in the Torah means a stranger, someone who lives among you, and the Torah is firm about the stranger: "The stranger that sojourneth with you shall be unto you as the home-born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The rabbis read that verse, among others, about converts. And the Mishnah sets a rule about words that wound: to someone from a family of converts, you may not say, remember what your ancestors did. You don't make them a guest in their own house. In Jewish law, once someone has converted, they are fully Jewish. Not almost. Not Jewish with a footnote. When a convert asked the medieval sage Maimonides whether he could say in the prayers, our God and God of our fathers, Maimonides answered yes: Abraham is his father too. And the book of Ruth ends with Ruth marrying Boaz; her great-grandson is David, the king. Israel's royal line runs through a woman from Moab who chose. Today people convert within each of the Jewish movements, after study, usually before a rabbinic court, and often with immersion in a ritual bath. The movements differ on the details and on whose conversions they accept, and those differences are real. But the rabbis' teaching is plain: a person who chose is not a lesser Jew.

1047.title: Every face
1047.hook: Jews of every color and background
1047.carry: a whole story, not a question
1047.howItsDone: Jewish communities and organizations share the histories of Ethiopian, Indian, Mizrahi, Sephardi, Ashkenazi and other Jews through study, festivals, food and personal stories, and some congregations make a point of welcoming Jews of color and Jews by choice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ger tzedek, the Jew by choice, and your line: fully Jewish. Today the welcome widens to the whole room.

"And a mixed multitude went up also with them." That's Exodus, on the night the Israelites walked out of Egypt: the text goes out of its way to say others walked out with them. Now step into a synagogue on a Saturday morning. The woman handing out prayer books may trace her family to Baghdad; the man beside you, to Addis Ababa, Kraków, Kochi, or a small town where nobody else was Jewish. A child in the front row was adopted. Someone at the back chose this people as an adult.
screen: `A MIXED MULTITUDE.` → `BAGHDAD, ADDIS ABABA, KRAKÓW, KOCHI.` → `ADOPTED, OR CHOSEN AS AN ADULT.`

segments.voice: The Mishnah asks a strange question. Why did God begin with just one person, one Adam, instead of a crowd? One of its answers: so nobody could ever say to anyone else, my ancestor was greater than yours. Everyone goes back to the same one. Then a picture from the mint: When a king stamps coins from one die, every coin comes out the same. God stamped every human being with the seal of the first person, and not one is like another. In this teaching, sameness is the human way of making things; difference is the divine signature. The prophet Amos goes further. Speaking for God to his own people, he asks: "Are ye not as the children of the Ethiopians unto Me, O children of Israel?" Readers hear it differently. Some hear a warning against pride: being chosen doesn't put you closer to God than a far-off nation. Others hear an embrace reaching all the way to Africa. Either way, the verse sets Israel and a distant people side by side in God's eyes. The faces of the Jewish people tell that story out loud: Beta Israel from Ethiopia, with their own prayers and the festival of Sigd; the Jews of Cochin in India; families from Yemen, Iraq, Morocco and Iran; Ashkenazi families from Europe; Jews by choice, and children of every color growing up in Jewish homes. Some Jews of color have described being asked, again and again, are you really Jewish? Yesterday already answered: someone who belongs, belongs. Each face is a whole story, not a question to be checked at the door.

segments.voice: Pick a Jewish community you know little about: Ethiopia, India, Yemen, Iran. You don't need answers; just make room, the way the Mishnah makes room for every face. If you pray, you can give thanks for the people of every look who belong.

1048.title: Cultural Jews
1048.hook: some Jews connect through culture, food, humor and history more than belief
1048.howItsDone: Some Jews express their Jewishness mostly through food, holidays at home, humor, language, books, music and history, and Jewish communities range from Humanistic congregations built on culture and ethics to Orthodox outreach that invites people toward more observance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, every face, and your line: a whole story, not a question. Today, a different kind of belonging.

A Friday night kitchen. Someone is braiding challah from a grandmother's recipe, flour up to the elbows. An uncle tells the same joke he told last year, and everyone groans on cue. A cousin who hasn't set foot in a synagogue in years is arguing hard about a piece of Jewish history. Ask any of them whether they believe in God, and you may get a shrug, a long story, or a laugh. Ask whether they're Jewish, and the answer comes fast: of course.
screen: `CHALLAH FROM GRANDMOTHER'S RECIPE.` → `THE SAME JOKE AS LAST YEAR.` → `JEWISH? OF COURSE.`

segments.voice: The Torah expects a question. About the Passover meal, Exodus says: "when your children shall say unto you: What mean ye by this service?" Not if. When. The tradition plans for the one who isn't sure what any of this is for. The Haggadah, the book read at the seder, turns that into four children. One is wise. One is called wicked, because he says this service is for you, not for him. One is simple. And one doesn't even know how to ask. All of them are at the table. The Haggadah has an answer for each, and for the child who can't ask, it tells the parent to open the conversation. Even the one called wicked gets an answer, a blunt one, and he is still counted among the four. Then a line from the Talmud that later rabbis leaned on: an Israelite, even one who has sinned, is still an Israelite. Some teachers read it as a statement about belonging that doubt doesn't switch off. That's why the Hebrew word am, a people, matters here. For some Jews, the way in isn't a creed. It's Yiddish words in a grandparent's mouth, a pot of soup, a shelf of books, a sense of humor, a history carried in the body. Communities respond in different ways. Humanistic Jewish congregations build their whole life around culture, history and ethics. Some Orthodox outreach teachers see the kitchen and the joke as a doorway, and gently invite people further in, toward Shabbat and the commandments. Others stand in between. Culture counts: it's one of the real ways people stay at the table.

1049.title: Interfaith families
1049.hook: some Jews live in interfaith families, and communities respond in different ways
1049.howItsDone: Jewish communities respond to interfaith families in different ways: Orthodox and Conservative communities follow descent through the mother and their rabbis generally do not officiate at interfaith weddings, while Reform and Reconstructionist communities accept a child of either Jewish parent raised as a Jew, and some of their rabbis officiate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cultural Jews, and your line: culture counts. Today, families where two traditions share one table.

A couple sits at a kitchen table with a notebook, planning a wedding. One of them is Jewish; the other isn't. The guest list is easy. The menu is easy. Then come the questions nobody wants to say out loud. Who will marry us? Under a chuppah, or not? And later, quietly: if we have children, what will they be? Their two families listen from a distance, hoping, worrying, loving them both. Jewish communities have been asked this for a long time, and they don't all give the same answer.
screen: `A NOTEBOOK AND A WEDDING.` → `WHO WILL MARRY US?` → `WHAT WILL THE CHILDREN BE?`

segments.voice: The Torah itself holds more than one view. Moses marries Zipporah, the daughter of Jethro, a priest of Midian. Later Jethro watches Moses judging the people from morning until evening, alone, worn down, and tells him to share the load: "So Moses hearkened to the voice of his father-in-law, and did all that he had said." The great lawgiver takes advice from a priest of another people. But the same Torah warns against marrying into the nations of Canaan, for fear the children will be turned away from God. And in the book of Ezra, returning exiles are told to send away foreign wives. The Bible doesn't settle it in one verse. The rabbis then made a rule about children: in the Mishnah, a child's Jewish status follows the mother. That rule still shapes communities, and they respond in different ways. Orthodox communities hold to traditional Jewish law: their rabbis don't officiate at interfaith weddings, and the child of a Jewish mother is Jewish. Conservative communities also follow the mother's line, and some reach out warmly to interfaith families who come through the door. Reform and Reconstructionist communities in North America accept a child with one Jewish parent, mother or father, who is raised as a Jew, and some of their rabbis officiate at interfaith weddings while others don't. Each holds its position for reasons it cares about: continuity, law, welcome, love. Meanwhile, real families live it. A non-Jewish parent drives the kids to Hebrew school every week. Grandparents learn new holidays. A child carries two sets of stories. Families are complex.

1050.title: Jewish humor
1050.hook: laughter as a way of surviving
1050.howItsDone: Jewish humor lives in family stories, folk tales, Yiddish and Ladino sayings, holiday spoofs such as Purim plays, and in writers and comedians, and it is often told by Jews about themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, interfaith families, and your line: families are complex. These last days were about who belongs: Jews by choice, every face, cultural Jews, families with two traditions. The week ends with a laugh.

A man is rescued after years alone on a desert island. His rescuers find he's built himself two synagogues. Why two, they ask. He points. This one I go to. That one, I wouldn't set foot in. People tell that joke at Jewish tables, about themselves. It's warm, a little sharp, and true enough to sting. It also hides something serious. A people that lived through exile, expulsions and grief kept something in its pocket the whole time: the ability to laugh, including at itself.
screen: `TWO SYNAGOGUES ON ONE ISLAND.` → `A JOKE TOLD ABOUT OURSELVES.` → `LAUGHTER KEPT IN THE POCKET.`

segments.voice: Laughter shows up early in the Torah, in an unexpected place. Sarah, old and long past hoping, overhears a visitor tell Abraham she'll have a son. She laughs to herself. When the child is born, she says God has made laughter for her, and everyone who hears will laugh with her. The boy is named Yitzchak, Isaac, and readers have long heard laughter in that name: a promise so unlikely the only honest answer was to laugh. The Psalms remember laughter at the other end of a hard road. A psalm about coming home from captivity says: "Then was our mouth filled with laughter." Not after everything was fixed. At the moment of return, still dusty. And the Talmud tells a small, lovely story. A rabbi named Beroka stands in a crowded market with the prophet Elijah and asks: is anyone here destined for the world to come? Elijah points to two ordinary men. The rabbi asks what they do. We're jesters, they say. When we see someone sad, we cheer them up. When we see two people quarreling, we work to make peace between them. In that whole crowded market, they're among the very few Elijah points to. In this tradition, humor at its best isn't a way of hiding from pain. It's a way of carrying it, and of carrying each other. A joke can let a frightened room breathe. It can puncture the pompous and spare the weak. It can say, we're still here.
screen: `SARAH LAUGHS.` · `THEN WAS OUR MOUTH FILLED WITH LAUGHTER.` · `TWO JESTERS IN THE MARKET.` · `HUMOR THAT CARRIES PAIN.` · then, large: `LAUGH.`

segments.voice: Go looking in memory for something that made you laugh: a family story, a line a friend said, something a child got gloriously wrong. Choose one that makes nobody smaller, and notice what it does to your face just to remember it. Then think of one person who could use it, someone tired or sad, the way the jesters in the market carried theirs.
